questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 1: Cell Injury
questions.stem: A 60-year-old man died of a massive renal infarct. Histology of the infarcted kidney would show:
questions.explanation:
Coagulative necrosis is the classic pattern of ischemic infarcts in all solid organs except the brain.

Hallmark features:
• Gross: wedge-shaped, pale infarct with a hyperemic border
• Micro: cell outlines and tissue architecture preserved for days — protein denaturation exceeds enzyme release
• Common sites: kidney, heart, spleen, liver

Why not the others:
• Liquefactive — brain infarcts and abscesses (lipid-rich tissue, powerful hydrolytic enzymes)
• Caseous — tuberculosis, granuloma caseation
• Fat — acute pancreatitis and traumatic fat necrosis

Mnemonic: SOLID organs show COAGULATIVE necrosis; the BRAIN liquefies
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 1; Robbins 9/e p43

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 1: Cell Injury
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most characteristic feature of apoptosis?

options.text: Cell swelling with bursting release of lysosomal enzymes
Cell shrinkage with membrane blebbing and no inflammation
Enzymatic digestion of fat by lipase

questions.answerText: Cell shrinkage with membrane blebbing and no inflammation
questions.explanation:
Apoptosis is programmed, energy-dependent single-cell death with minimal inflammation — the dead cell simply packs itself neatly for phagocytosis.

Hallmark features:
• Cell shrinkage with cytoplasmic membrane blebbing
• Nuclear: chromatin condensation (pyknosis) and fragmentation (karyorrhexis)
• Executioners: caspase cascade (initiator caspase-8 and 9, effector caspase-3)
• Membrane stays intact — inflammatory mediators are never released
• hallmark on EM: surface blebs and apoptotic bodies engulfed by macrophages

Key contrast with necrosis: necrosis = cell swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation

Mnemonic: APOPTOSIS = Atomic (single cell), Packed (blebs), Orderly, No inflammation
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 1; Robbins 9/e p26

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 1: Cell Injury
questions.stem: Reperfusion injury following myocardial infarction is chiefly mediated by:

options.text: Reactive oxygen species with calcium overload
Defect in membrane permeability of potassium

questions.answerText: Reactive oxygen species with calcium overload
questions.explanation:
Restoration of blood flow is a double-edged sword — the reperfused tissue gets a fresh burst of injury mediators.

Mechanism of reperfusion injury:
• Oxidative stress — huge surge of reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydroxyl radical) from re-energized mitochondria and infiltrating neutrophils
• Calcium overload — damaged mitochondria cannot pump Ca2+ out, worsening ATP depletion
• Inflammation — cytokines and complement recruited by the sudden blood return
• Activation of mitochondrial permeability transition pore → apoptosis

Clinical correlate: no-reflow phenomenon and lethal reperfusion arrhythmias

Mnemonic: Reperfusion = ROS + Refilled calcium (both begin with R)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 1; Robbins 9/e p23

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 1: Cell Injury
questions.stem: Calcification of atheromatous plaques and healed tuberculous lesions with normal serum calcium is called:
questions.explanation:
Dystrophic calcification means calcium salt deposition in DEAD or DYING tissue despite a NORMAL serum calcium — a local problem, not a systemic one.

Classic sites:
• Atheromatous plaques, damaged heart valves
• Healed TB lesions, old infarcts, hyalinized scars
• Necrotic fat in panniculitis

Contrast with metastatic calcification:
• Deposition in HEALTHY tissue due to HYPERCALCEMIA (hyperparathyroidism, bone destruction, vitamin D toxicity, renal failure)
• Favors calcium-excreting sites — kidneys, lungs, gastric mucosa

Mnemonic: Dystrophic = Diseased tissue, D-normal calcium; Metastatic = Moving everywhere with high calcium
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 1; Robbins 9/e p65

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 1: Cell Injury
questions.stem: A brown, shrunken heart of an elderly person shows granular yellow-brown pigment that stains with Schmorl's stain. The pigment is:
questions.explanation:
Lipofuscin is the wear-and-tear or aging pigment — an insoluble stash of lipid-protein residues that lysosomes could not fully digest.

Key features:
• Color: yellow-brown, finely granular, perinuclear
• Sites: heart (brown atrophy), liver, testis, neurons of elderly
• stains: fat-soluble, Schmorl positive, PAS positive, impermeable to bleaching
• Significance: harmless companion of aging and free-radical injury

Why not the others:
• Hemosiderin — coarse golden, Prussian blue positive, from iron overload
• Melanin — black, bleaches with hydrogen peroxide, from melanocytes
• Bilirubin — green-black pigment of bile, seen in jaundice

Mnemonic: LIPUSCIN = LIPid + fuSCIN-ness of old age (brown aging pigment)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 1; Robbins 9/e p64

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 2: Inflammation
questions.stem: The earliest mediator of increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation is:
questions.explanation:
Histamine released from mast cell degranulation is the FIRST responder — it acts within minutes of injury.

Actions of histamine:
• Arteriolar vasodilation (the flare of the triple response)
• Immediate transient increase in venular endothelial contraction → gap formation → permeability
• Mediates the early part of the Lewis triple response (red line, flare, wheal)

Timeline of permeability mediators:
• 0–30 min: histamine, serotonin (preformed, immediate)
• 30 min–hours: bradykinin, leukotrienes C4/D4/E4, PAF
• Sustained: direct endothelial injury, delayed prolonged leakage (sunburn type)

Mnemonic: Histamine Hurries in first — H for Hurry
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 2; Robbins 9/e p72

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 2: Inflammation
questions.stem: All of the following are opsonins EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Opsonins are molecular velcro that coat microbes so phagocytes can grab them via their receptors.

True opsonins:
• C3b — binds complement receptor 1 on neutrophils and macrophages
• IgG Fc portion — binds Fc receptors
• C-reactive protein — pentraxin that opsonizes and also fixes complement
• Mannose-binding lectin and collectins also act as opsonins

Why C3a is not an opsonin:
• C3a is an ANAPHYLATOXIN (with C4a and C5a) — it triggers mast cell degranulation
• C5a is also a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, but again not an opsonin

Mnemonic: Opsonins = C3b, Antibody, CRP (the AC scheme); the a-fragments (C3a/C5a) cause Anaphylaxis
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 2; Robbins 9/e p76

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 2: Inflammation
questions.stem: Asteroid bodies and Schaumann bodies within granulomas are characteristic of:
questions.explanation:
Sarcoidosis produces NON-CASEATING granulomas with characteristic cytoplasmic inclusions inside multinucleate giant cells.

Inclusions of sarcoid granulomas:
• Asteroid bodies — star-shaped crystalline inclusions
• Schaumann bodies — laminated conchoidal (shell-like) calcium-impregnated bodies
• Hamazaki-Wesenberg bodies — giant lysosomes

Key contrast with TB:
• TB granuloma — caseating, central necrosis, acid-fast bacilli, Langhans giant cells
• Sarcoid — non-caseating, tight (naked) granulomas, no necrosis, CD4+ Th1 driven

Note: these inclusions are characteristic, not pathognomonic — they can appear in other granulomas too, so correlate clinically (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, raised ACE, noncaseating granulomas).

Mnemonic: Sarcoid Shoots Stars and Shells (asteroid and Schaumann)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 2; Robbins 9/e p388

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 2: Inflammation
questions.stem: The classic bread-and-butter appearance of the pericardium in pericarditis represents which type of inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Fibrinous inflammation occurs when a severe injury lets fibrinogen escape the vessels and clot on a serosal surface — the two roughened surfaces rub like a slice of buttered bread.

Characteristics of fibrinous exudate:
• Vascular permeability is so great that fibrinogen passes through
• Deposits a shaggy eosinophilic fibrin mesh on pericardium, pleura, or alveoli
• Common causes: uremia, acute MI (Dressler), rheumatic fever, rheumatoid arthritis
• Auscultation: pericardial friction rub

Resolution possibilities:
• Fibrinolysis restores the surface completely
• Organization by fibroblasts → fibrous adhesions or constrictive pericarditis

Mnemonic: FIBRINous = FRICTION rub + Bread-and-Butter (both foods need a rough surface)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 2; Robbins 9/e p73

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 2: Inflammation
questions.stem: The hallmark cell of chronic inflammation is:
questions.explanation:
The macrophage is the jack-of-all-trades of chronic inflammation — it kills, cleans, presents antigen, and builds tissue.

Why macrophage rules chronicity:
• Derived from blood monocytes recruited via MCP-1 and adhesion molecules
• Produces the full cytokine arsenal — IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-12, TGF-beta
• Classical activation (IFN-gamma from Th1 cells) → microbicidal M1 state
• Alternative activation (IL-4, IL-13 from Th2) → repair and fibrosis M2 state
• Can fuse to form Langhans or foreign-body giant cells

Supporting cast in chronic inflammation:
• Lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils, mast cells

Mnemonic: Chronicity needs the Big MACrophage — the Neutrophil only does acute shift work
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 2; Robbins 9/e p78

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 3: Hemodynamics
questions.stem: Edema in nephrotic syndrome is best explained by:

options.text: Increased sodium retention secondary to hyperaldosteronism alone

questions.explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome drains albumin into the urine, and the plasma loses the oncotic pull that normally holds water inside vessels.

Starling forces in nephrotic edema:
• Heavy proteinuria (>3.5 g/day) → hypoalbuminemia
• Decreased plasma oncotic (colloid osmotic) pressure → water slides into interstitium
• Secondary compensation: hypovolemia triggers RAAS → aldosterone-driven sodium retention, which worsens edema
• Result: periorbital and generalized (anasarca) edema

Compare with other mechanisms:
• Increased hydrostatic pressure — cardiac failure, DVT
• Lymphatic obstruction — filariasis, post-surgical, malignancy
• Sodium retention alone — Cushing, renal artery stenosis

Mnemonic: NEPHROTIC = Protein Leaks, ONCotic pressure Drops
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 3; Robbins 9/e p122

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 3: Hemodynamics
questions.stem: The most sensitive laboratory indicator of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is:
questions.explanation:
DIC is a thrombo-hemorrhagic storm — widespread microthrombi consume platelets and factors, then fibrinolysis kicks in. D-dimer catches the fibrin breakdown happening in real time.

DIC workup hierarchy:
• Most sensitive: elevated D-dimer (fibrin degradation product) — it is the smoking gun of ongoing fibrinolysis
• Also elevated: fibrin degradation products (FDP)
• Consumed: platelets, fibrinogen, factors — so PT, aPTT and thrombin time prolong and platelets fall
• Blood film: microangiopathic picture with schistocytes and helmet cells

Clinical triggers: sepsis (endotoxin), obstetric catastrophes, AML-M3, snake bite, major trauma

Mnemonic: D for DIC, D for Dimer — the most sensitive Duo
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 3; Robbins 9/e p128

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 3: Hemodynamics
questions.stem: All of the following are components of Virchow's triad EXCEPT:

options.text: Stasis or turbulence of blood flow

questions.explanation:
Virchow's triad is the three-part recipe for thrombosis — more fibrinolysis would actually protect against clots, so it sits outside the triad.

Virchow's triad:
• Endothelial injury — the dominant factor in arterial and cardiac thrombi (hypertension, atheroma)
• Abnormal blood flow — stasis (postoperative bed rest, atrial fibrillation) or turbulence (over ulcerated plaques)
• Hypercoagulability — factor V Leiden, oral contraceptives, malignancy (Trousseau syndrome), antiphospholipid syndrome

Why the wrong option is wrong:
• Increased fibrinolytic activity would lyse clots — thrombosis needs the opposite (hypofibrinolysis)

Mnemonic: Virchow Wants Vessels damaged, Flow slowed, Blood sticky
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 3; Robbins 9/e p116

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 3: Hemodynamics
questions.stem: A 25-year-old man develops tachypnea, confusion and petechial hemorrhages over the chest 36 hours after a femoral shaft fracture. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Long-bone fractures push marrow fat into the venous system, and the clinical picture erupts 24–72 hours later.

Fat embolism syndrome triad:
• Respiratory distress — tachypnea, hypoxemia, acute lung injury
• Neurological symptoms — confusion, seizures, coma (petechiae in cerebral microvasculature)
• Petechial rash — chest, axilla, conjunctivae; pathognomonic and usually transient

Key mechanisms:
• Mechanical obstruction of pulmonary capillaries by fat globules
• Biochemical injury — free fatty acids damage pneumocytes and endothelium

Prevention: early immobilization of the fracture
Contrast: pulmonary thromboembolism presents with hemodynamic collapse rather than petechiae and delayed neurology

Mnemonic: Fat embolism FRactures create Fat, Faulty lungs, Fuzzy brain and Freckles (petechiae)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 3; Robbins 9/e p129

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 4: Genetics
questions.stem: The basic defect in Marfan syndrome lies in:
questions.explanation:
Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by FBN1 gene mutations on chromosome 15 encoding fibrillin-1.

Clinical features:
• Skeletal — tall stature, arm span exceeds height, arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum or carinatum, high-arched palate
• Ocular — upward lens SUBLUXATION (ectopia lentis), myopia, retinal detachment
• Cardiovascular — aortic root dilation, aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection (life-threatening complication and the usual cause of death)

Why not the others:
• Collagen I — osteogenesis imperfecta
• Collagen IV — Alport syndrome
• Elastin — cutis laxa and supravalvular aortic stenosis

Mnemonic: Marfan = Misplaced Fibrillin (chr 15, 1-5 like F-1)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 4; Robbins 9/e p142

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 4: Genetics
questions.stem: Anticipation in Huntington disease is due to expansion of which trinucleotide repeat?
questions.explanation:
Huntington disease is the classic CAG polyglutamine repeat disorder — each generation inherits a longer run of CAG, and the disease strikes earlier and harder (anticipation).

Repeat disorders at a glance:
• CAG (polyglutamine) — Huntington, spinocerebellar ataxias, Kennedy disease — all gain-of-function, all anticipation
• CGG — fragile X syndrome (FMR1), most common inherited intellectual disability
• CTG — myotonic dystrophy
• GAA — Friedreich ataxia

Huntington specifics:
• Gene: huntingtin on chromosome 4
• Caudate and putamen atrophy with normal-pressure hydrocephalus-like ventricular ballooning
• Chorea plus psychiatric and cognitive decline

Mnemonic: CAG = Chorea And Glutamine (repeats grow, disease grows — Codon AGgregation)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 4; Robbins 9/e p168

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 4: Genetics
questions.stem: The most common mutation causing cystic fibrosis is:
questions.explanation:
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disease of the CFTR chloride channel, and the three-base-pair deletion removing phenylalanine 508 (delta-F508) accounts for roughly 70% of mutant alleles worldwide.

CFTR defect consequences:
• Defective chloride conductance → dehydrated, viscous secretions everywhere
• Lungs — recurrent Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus infections, bronchiectasis
• Pancreas — pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus in neonates, diabetes
• Sweat glands — elevated sweat chloride (the diagnostic sweat chloride test)

Diagnosis: sweat chloride >60 mmol/L plus genetic testing of the CFTR gene on chromosome 7

Mnemonic: F for Fifty, F for Fibrosis — delta-F508 is the First answer
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 4; Robbins 9/e p468

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 4: Genetics
questions.stem: A child with obesity, hypogonadism and intellectual disability has a deletion on chromosome 15q11 inherited from the father. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Prader-Willi and Angelman are the textbook demonstration of genomic imprinting — the same 15q11-13 locus behaves differently depending on which parent it came from.

Imprinting at 15q11-13:
• PATERNAL deletion → Prader-Willi — hypotonia in infancy, obesity, hyperphagia, hypogonadism, intellectual disability
• MATERNAL deletion → Angelman — happy puppet syndrome, ataxia, severe intellectual disability, inappropriate laughter, seizures

Mechanism: only one parental allele is active at this locus because the other is methylated; losing the active one causes disease

Mnemonic: PW = Paternal Will(i) — the father passes the fat gene; Angel comes from Mom (maternal = Angelman)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 4; Robbins 9/e p172

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 5: Neoplasia
questions.stem: The gene located on chromosome 17p, called the guardian of the genome, is:
questions.explanation:
TP53 on 17p is the guardian of the genome — the most commonly mutated gene in all human cancers.

What p53 does when DNA is damaged:
• Arrests the cell cycle at G1-S checkpoint via p21 induction
• Drives DNA repair
• Initiates apoptosis (bax) if damage is beyond repair
• Being a tumor suppressor, both alleles must be knocked out (two-hit) for cancer — except in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, where one inherited mutant p53 predisposes to sarcomas, breast cancer, leukemia and adrenocortical carcinoma

Why not the others:
• RB1 — 13q, retinoblastoma
• BRCA1 — 17q, breast and ovarian cancer (same chromosome, different arm!)
• APC — 5q, familial adenomatous polyposis

Mnemonic: p53 on 17p — both are a prime (p) number; Li-Fraumeni Luggage = Sarcoma, Breast, Leukemia, Adrenal
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 5; Robbins 9/e p294

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 5: Neoplasia
questions.stem: The most commonly mutated oncogene in human tumors is:
questions.explanation:
RAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancer — found mutated in roughly 15–20% of all tumors and up to 90% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas.

How RAS turns malignant:
• A membrane-bound GTP-binding signal transducer that normally flips between active GTP and inactive GDP states
• Mutations abolish GTPase activity (codons 12, 13, 61) — the switch jams ON
• Constitutive signaling through the MAPK cascade → uncontrolled proliferation
• Its cofactor path: mutated RAS plus inactivated TGF-beta signaling is the classic colon cancer combination

Why not the others:
• MYC — Burkitt lymphoma t(8;14), overexpression not point mutation
• HER2 — breast cancer amplification
• ABL — CML fusion with BCR

Mnemonic: RAS Runs All Sorts of cancers (R for the Record holder)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 5; Robbins 9/e p289

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 5: Neoplasia
questions.stem: Philadelphia chromosome seen in chronic myeloid leukemia results from:
questions.explanation:
The Philadelphia chromosome is a shortened chromosome 22 created by reciprocal translocation t(9;22) — the signature of chronic myeloid leukemia.

BCR-ABL fusion biology:
• c-ABL kinase from chromosome 9 fuses with BCR from chromosome 22
• The fusion protein has constitutive tyrosine kinase activity driving myeloproliferation
• Targeted therapy: imatinib mesylate — a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that changed CML survival dramatically

Distinguish the other translocations:
• t(8;14) — Burkitt lymphoma, MYC overexpression
• t(15;17) — acute promyelocytic leukemia M3, PML-RAR alpha, treated with ATRA
• t(11;14) — mantle cell lymphoma, cyclin D1

Mnemonic: 9 plus 22 = 31 → CML has 3 letters 1 drug (imatinib); Philadelphia = Power(9) + C(22)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 5; Robbins 9/e p290

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 5: Neoplasia
questions.stem: Tumor marker AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) is characteristically elevated in:
questions.explanation:
Alpha-fetoprotein is the oncofetal antigen of hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumors.

Tumor marker quick map:
• AFP — hepatocellular carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, some metastatic liver disease
• CA 19-9 — pancreatic adenocarcinoma
• PSA — prostatic adenocarcinoma
• CA-125 — ovarian epithelial (especially serous) carcinoma
• CEA — colorectal and other adenocarcinomas
• Beta-hCG — choriocarcinoma, germ cell tumors

Clinical caution:
• AFP also rises in pregnancy, fetal neural tube defects and cirrhosis — specificity for HCC improves markedly when it exceeds 400 ng/mL in a cirrhotic liver with a space-occupying lesion

Mnemonic: AFP = A Fetal Protein returning in Liver cancer and Yolk sac tumor
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 5; Robbins 9/e p300

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 5: Neoplasia
questions.stem: The most common route of metastasis of carcinomas is:
questions.explanation:
Carcinomas (epithelial tumors) love the lymphatics — lymph node spread is the rule — whereas sarcomas prefer the bloodstream.

Spread patterns:
• Carcinoma — lymphatic spread first (e.g., breast cancer to axillary nodes, gastric cancer to Virchow node)
• Sarcoma — hematogenous spread first (e.g., osteosarcoma to lungs)
• Transcoelomic — ovarian cancer seeding peritoneum (pseudomyxoma and peritoneal implants), lung cancer to pleura
• Perineural — prostate, pancreatic and adenoid cystic carcinoma (a hallmark)

Classic lymphatic landmarks:
• Virchow (sentinel) node — left supraclavicular, gastric and other abdominal cancers
• Sister Mary Joseph nodule — periumbilical metastasis

Mnemonic: CARcinoma rides the LYMPH; SARcoma swims in the BLOOD
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 5; Robbins 9/e p280

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 6: Immunity
questions.stem: Goodpasture syndrome involving glomerular and alveolar basement membranes is an example of which hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.explanation:
Goodpasture syndrome is the classic Type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity against the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.

Type II hypersensitivity essentials:
• Antibodies (IgG, IgM) target fixed cell or matrix antigens
• Mechanisms: complement-mediated lysis, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, receptor blockade or activation
• Examples: autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Goodpasture, Graves disease (receptor activation), myasthenia gravis (receptor blockade), pemphigus vulgaris

Why not the others:
• Type I — IgE-mediated anaphylaxis
• Type III — immune-complex diseases (SLE, PSGN, serum sickness)
• Type IV — T-cell mediated (Mantoux, contact dermatitis)

Mnemonic: Goodpasture = anti-BM Antibody = Type II (the body attacks its own Basement Membrane)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 6; Robbins 9/e p206

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 6: Immunity
questions.stem: A 30-year-old nurse develops itchy vesicular dermatitis on the hands after wearing latex gloves. The underlying mechanism is:

options.text: CD4 and CD8 T-cell mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity

questions.answerText: CD4 and CD8 T-cell mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity
questions.explanation:
Contact dermatitis from latex, nickel, poison ivy or haptens is the prototype of Type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity — a T-cell story, not an antibody story.

Type IV hypersensitivity mechanics:
• Sensitization phase — hapten processed by Langerhans cells, presented to CD4+ T cells in draining nodes
• Effector phase — re-exposure recruits CD4+ Th1 cells releasing IFN-gamma plus CD8+ cytotoxic cells killing antigen-bearing keratinocytes
• Response peaks at 48–72 hours — hence delayed
• Mantoux tuberculin test follows the same pathway

Contrast with IgE-mediated latex allergy (Type I):
• True latex allergy with urticaria, angioedema and anaphylaxis is Type I — but the itchy vesicular hand eczema of a nurse is the T-cell delayed form

Mnemonic: Type IV = T-cells, Time-delayed (48–72 h), Touch dermatitis
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 6; Robbins 9/e p212

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 6: Immunity
questions.stem: The most common cause of autosomal recessive severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is:
questions.explanation:
SCID is a devastating combined B and T cell immunodeficiency of infancy, and among autosomal recessive cases ADA deficiency leads the list.

ADA deficiency mechanism:
• Loss of adenosine deaminase lets deoxyadenosine and dATP accumulate
• These metabolites are especially toxic to dividing lymphocyte precursors — T cells die first, then B cells
• Presentation: recurrent severe infections (oral candidiasis, Pneumocystis pneumonia, persistent diarrhea) in the first months of life
• Treatment: enzyme replacement with PEG-ADA, bone marrow transplant, and gene therapy (a landmark success)

Note the distinction:
• Most common AR SCID — ADA deficiency
• Most common overall SCID — X-linked IL-2 receptor gamma chain (IL2RG) defect

Mnemonic: ADA = Autosomal Deficiency of Adenosine deaminase; the X is the X-linked IL-2R
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 6; Robbins 9/e p238

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 6: Immunity
questions.stem: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
HLA-B27 is the seronegative spondyloarthropathy antigen — rheumatoid arthritis belongs to a different family and carries HLA-DR4 instead.

Diseases associated with HLA-B27:
• Ankylosing spondylitis (over 90% positive)
• Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome — can't see, pee, or climb a tree)
• Psoriatic arthritis (axial form)
• Enteropathic arthritis with IBD
• Acute anterior uveitis

Contrast associations:
• Rheumatoid arthritis — HLA-DR4
• Celiac disease — HLA-DQ2 and DQ8
• Narcolepsy — HLA-DQB1

Mnemonic: PAIR of B27 diseases — Psoriasis, Ankylosing, IBD-related, Reactive (the spondylo-PAIR-thies); RA Runs Alone with DR4
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 6; Robbins 9/e p227

questions.chapter: Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.stem: The most sensitive and specific indicator of iron deficiency anemia is:
questions.explanation:
Serum ferritin mirrors the iron stores of the body — it falls first, long before anemia appears, making it the single best test.

Iron panel in deficiency:
• Serum ferritin — decreased (most sensitive and specific; <15 ng/mL diagnostic)
• Serum iron — decreased
• TIBC — increased (empty transport slots hunting for iron)
• Transferrin saturation — decreased (<16%)
• RDW — increased (anisocytosis), peripheral smear — microcytic hypochromic with pencil cells

Important trap: ferritin is an acute phase reactant — it is falsely NORMAL or elevated in coexisting inflammation, liver disease or the anemia of chronic disease

Mnemonic: Ferritin = the body's First-class iron bank statement (low = empty account)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 7; Robbins 9/e p649

questions.chapter: Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with mild anemia has hemoglobin electrophoresis showing HbA2 of 6.5% (normal 2.5–3.5%). The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
A mildly anemic, asymptomatic person with raised HbA2 above 3.5% is the classic picture of beta thalassemia minor (trait) — one defective beta-globin allele.

Electrophoresis patterns:
• Beta thalassemia minor — HbA2 increased (3.5–8%), HbF mildly raised, mild microcytic anemia, target cells, no transfusion need
• Beta thalassemia major (Cooley anemia) — little or no HbA, massive HbF, transfusion dependent, skeletal deformities, iron overload
• Alpha thalassemia trait — normal electrophoresis (diagnosed by exclusion or genetic testing)

Why not the others:
• Major — presents in infancy with severe anemia, not a mild incidental finding at 20
• Alpha trait — HbA2 is normal, not elevated
• HPFH — high HbF, but HbA2 not elevated in this pattern

Mnemonic: Beta-2-Minor — the MINOR trait carries a raised HbA2 near 2x normal
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 7; Robbins 9/e p656

questions.chapter: Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.stem: Sickle cell disease results from substitution of valine for glutamic acid at which position of the beta-globin chain?
questions.explanation:
A single point mutation (GAG to GTG) replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain — the smallest change with one of the biggest clinical footprints in medicine.

Pathophysiology cascade:
• Valine is hydrophobic — it fits into a pocket on a neighboring deoxygenated hemoglobin
• Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into tactoids, sickling the red cell
• Sickled cells block microcirculation (vaso-occlusive crises) and are destroyed prematurely (hemolysis)
• Repeated cycles fragment the membrane — irreversibly sickled cells appear

Protective note: the sickle trait confers protection against falciparum malaria — a textbook balanced polymorphism

Mnemonic: Sickle = GAG to GTG at 6 — Glu leaves, Valine Visits (position 6, like a 6-shooter)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 7; Robbins 9/e p638

questions.chapter: Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.stem: A 45-year-old vegetarian presents with macrocytic anemia, glossitis and paresthesias of the feet with loss of vibration sense. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Neurological involvement is the tie-breaker between B12 and folate deficiency — only B12 deficiency attacks the spinal cord.

Vitamin B12 deficiency picture:
• Blood — macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes), high LDH and indirect bilirubin from ineffective erythropoiesis
• Neurology — subacute combined degeneration: demyelination of dorsal (vibration, proprioception) and lateral corticospinal columns
• Mouth — glossy sore tongue (glossitis)
• Sources — only animal products; vegetarians and pernicious anemia (anti-intrinsic factor antibodies) are at risk

Why folate is wrong: folate deficiency causes identical anemia and glossitis but NO neurological deficits

Mnemonic: B12 = Both anemia and Back-cord (subacute combined degeneration); Folate Fails the neuro test
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 7; Robbins 9/e p665

questions.chapter: Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 7: Anemia and Red Blood Cells
questions.stem: An elevated MCHC with spherocytes on peripheral smear and increased osmotic fragility suggests:
questions.explanation:
Hereditary spherocytosis is the most common inherited membrane defect of red cells in northern Europeans, and an abnormally HIGH MCHC is its fingerprint (almost the only anemia where MCHC rises).

Defect and diagnosis:
• Defective spectrin and ankyrin — vertical linkages of the membrane skeleton fail
• Membrane is lost as blebs, cell rounds into a sphere with minimum surface area
• Osmotic fragility increased — spherocytes burst in salt concentrations normal cells tolerate
• EMA (eosin-5-maleimide) binding test is the modern screening test; splenectomy is the definitive treatment

Why not the others:
• AIHA — spherocytes too, but Coombs test positive (HS is Coombs negative)
• G6PD — bite cells and Heinz bodies after oxidant stress
• Sickle — sickled cells, not spherocytes

Mnemonic: HS = High MCHC + Spherocytes (and the spleen is the culprit organ)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 7; Robbins 9/e p632

questions.chapter: Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.stem: Neutrophilic leukocytosis with a high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score suggests:
questions.explanation:
The LAP score is the classic discriminator between a benign neutrophil reaction and chronic myeloid leukemia — infection pushes LAP up, CML pushes it down.

Leukemoid reaction versus CML:
• Leukemoid — LAP score HIGH, toxic granules and Dohle bodies, normal cytogenetics, driven by infection or inflammation
• CML — LAP score LOW, Philadelphia chromosome positive, basophilia and splenomegaly, uncontrolled BCR-ABL

Supporting clues for leukemoid:
• Neutrophil count rarely exceeds 50,000/uL
• No anemia or thrombocytopenia
• Resolves when the underlying infection is treated

Mnemonic: Leukemoid = Leukocytes Are Plenty (LAP High); CML = Cells Look Miserable (LAP Low)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 8; Robbins 9/e p614

questions.chapter: Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.stem: The first-line treatment for chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in adults is:
questions.explanation:
ITP is an autoimmune destruction of platelets by anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies, and corticosteroids are the standard first-line therapy.

Treatment ladder for adult ITP:
• First line — corticosteroids (prednisone); response usually within 1–3 weeks
• Rescue or urgent — IVIG and anti-D immunoglobulin (block Fc receptors, raise count within 24–48 hours)
• Second line — splenectomy (removes both the antibody factory and the platelet graveyard), rituximab, thrombopoietin agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim)

Diagnostic anchors:
• Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal bone marrow (increased megakaryocytes)
• Bleeding time prolonged; PT and aPTT normal (clotting factors untouched)

Mnemonic: Steroids are the Standard Step one; Spleen is the Second Step; Serum IVIG is the Stopgap
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 8; Robbins 9/e p661

questions.chapter: Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.stem: A patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia has the translocation t(15;17). The gene fusion involved is:
questions.explanation:
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (FAB AML-M3) carries t(15;17), fusing the PML gene on 15 with the retinoic acid receptor alpha on 17.

Why the fusion matters clinically:
• The PML-RAR alpha fusion blocks myeloid differentiation at the promyelocyte stage
• All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) binds the fusion and unlocks differentiation — the leukemic cells finally mature and then die
• ATRA plus arsenic trioxide converts the once-lethal M3 into one of the most curable leukemias
• M3 is also notorious for life-threatening DIC from tissue-factor-rich promyelocyte granules

Why not the others:
• BCR-ABL — CML and Philadelphia chromosome
• AML1-ETO — AML-M2 with t(8;21)
• MYC-IgH — Burkitt lymphoma

Mnemonic: M3 = 15 plus 17 = 32 → Differentiation Door Dbl-locked; ATRA is the Key
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 8; Robbins 9/e p620

questions.chapter: Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 8: White Blood Cells and Platelets
questions.stem: Reed-Sternberg cells, the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma, are derived from:
questions.explanation:
Despite rarely expressing normal B cell markers cleanly, Reed-Sternberg cells are malignant germinal center B lymphocytes that lost most of their B cell program.

Reed-Sternberg cell essentials:
• Large binucleate or multinucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli
• Immunophenotype: CD15 and CD30 positive, CD20 usually negative or weak
• Often infected by Epstein-Barr virus — its genome is found in a substantial subset
• Surrounding reactive infiltrate (lymphocytes, plasma cells, eosinophils) makes up the bulk of the tumor mass — the RS cells recruit it by cytokines

Clinical anchor: the infiltrate burden correlates with the B symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats) of Hodgkin lymphoma

Mnemonic: RS = Really (a) Suppressed B cell wearing CD15 + CD30 badges
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 8; Robbins 9/e p603

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 9: Cardiovascular System
questions.stem: The most common site of atherosclerotic plaque formation is:
questions.explanation:
Atherosclerosis is patchy and picks hemodynamic hot spots — and the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries tops the list.

Site hierarchy of atherosclerosis:
• Most common — abdominal aorta (hence the frequency of AAA and Leriche syndrome)
• Coronary arteries — LAD > RCA > LCx (proximal segments at branch points)
• Popliteal and femoral, internal carotid, circle of Willis

Why branch points and the abdominal aorta:
• Low shear stress and turbulent flow at bifurcations disturb endothelial function
• Longer residence time of LDL at flow separation zones

Earliest lesion: fatty streak — visible in the aorta of virtually all children by adolescence

Mnemonic: Atherosclerosis Abhors the Abdominal Aorta — Abdominal first, then branches
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 9; Robbins 9/e p494

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 9: Cardiovascular System
questions.stem: The most commonly involved valve in chronic rheumatic heart disease is:
questions.explanation:
The mitral valve bears the brunt of rheumatic fever — it faces the highest pressure and flow stress of all four valves.

Valve involvement in rheumatic heart disease:
• Mitral alone — 65–70% of cases
• Mitral plus aortic — about 25% (combined involvement)
• Aortic alone — rare; tricuspid and pulmonary involvement rarer still (low-pressure valves)

Chronic changes of the mitral valve:
• Fish-mouth or buttonhole stenosis from commissural fusion
• Leaflet thickening, chordal shortening and calcification
• MacCallum patch — endocardial thickening in the left atrium

Remember the acute phase: Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells (caterpillar nuclei) with verrucous (sterile) endocarditis along leaflet closure lines

Mnemonic: Mitral = Most affected (it takes the Most pressure — first M's match)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 9; Robbins 9/e p558

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 9: Cardiovascular System
questions.stem: The most common organism causing infective endocarditis in an intravenous drug abuser is:
questions.explanation:
In the IV drug abuser, Staphylococcus aureus rides in on dirty needles and attacks the RIGHT side of the heart.

Endocarditis organism map:
• IV drug abuser — Staphylococcus aureus, tricuspid valve, right-sided vegetations with septic pulmonary emboli
• Subacute (native valve, damaged) — viridans streptococci after dental procedures
• Prosthetic valve early (<2 months) — coagulase-negative staphylococci
• Prosthetic valve late — viridans and Staphylococcus aureus
• Subacute with negative cultures — HACEK organisms (slow growers)

Clinical tip: right-sided endocarditis presents with recurrent pneumonia rather than the classic peripheral stigmata — so keep a high index of suspicion in any febrile drug abuser

Mnemonic: Drugs Deliver Destructive aureus to the Dorsal (right) side
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 9; Robbins 9/e p565

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 9: Cardiovascular System
questions.stem: Berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis are most strongly associated with which inherited disorder?
questions.explanation:
Autosomal dominant (adult) polycystic kidney disease and berry aneurysms are inseparable — about 10–30% of ADPKD patients harbor one, and rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Berry aneurysm essentials:
• Saccular outpouching at branch points of the circle of Willis, most often at the anterior communicating artery
• Rupture presents as the worst headache of my life with sudden sentinel headache and subarachnoid hemorrhage
• Risk factors: hypertension, cigarette smoking, female sex, family history

ADPKD connection:
• Autosomal dominant PKD1 (16p) and PKD2 mutations, cysts progressively destroy kidneys
• Associated extras: hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula and intracranial berry aneurysms

Mnemonic: ADPKD = A Deadly Pair of Kidneys and a Berry in the Brain
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 9; Robbins 9/e p506

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 10: Respiratory System
questions.stem: A stone-cutter presents with progressive dyspnea. Chest X-ray shows eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is the signature of silicosis — crystalline quartz dust from stone cutting, mining, sandblasting and pottery.

Silicosis features:
• Upper lobe predominant nodular fibrosis with concentric silicotic nodules (whorled collagen)
• Eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes — highly characteristic
• Increased susceptibility to tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis) and lung cancer
• Macrophages ingest quartz, die, and hand the dust back — a self-sustaining loop

Why not the others:
• Asbestosis — lower lobe interstitial fibrosis with pleural plaques and asbestos bodies
• Coal worker's — coal macules, progressive massive fibrosis, no eggshell calcification
• Berylliosis — non-caseating granulomas resembling sarcoidosis

Mnemonic: Silica = Stone-cutter with Shell-shaped (eggshell) nodes; asbestos = plaques
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 10; Robbins 9/e p690

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 10: Respiratory System
questions.stem: A retired shipyard worker has lower-lobe interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaques and ferruginous bodies in sputum. Exposure to which agent explains these findings?
questions.explanation:
Asbestos exposure links pleural plaques, lower-lobe fibrosis and ferruginous (asbestos) bodies — and importantly, it is the only pneumoconiosis that raises the risk of mesothelioma.

Asbestosis package:
• Pleural plaques — ivory-white, calcified, on parietal pleura and diaphragm (the most common finding)
• Lower-lobe interstitial fibrosis — coarse honeycombing
• Asbestos (ferruginous) bodies — beaded, dumbbell-shaped, golden iron-coated fibers
• Malignancy: bronchogenic carcinoma actually outnumbers mesothelioma; both are elevated

Why not the others:
• Silica — upper lobe nodules, eggshell nodal calcification
• Beryllium — granulomatous disease like sarcoid
• Coal dust — coal macules and progressive massive fibrosis, no pleural plaques

Mnemonic: Asbestos Attacks the Apex of the Pleura (plaques) but sits LOW in the lungs — the opposite of silica
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 10; Robbins 9/e p691

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 10: Respiratory System
questions.stem: A 60-year-old smoker with a central lung mass develops hyponatremia with high urine sodium and euvolemic hyponatremia. The most likely tumor type is:
questions.explanation:
Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma is the paraneoplastic champion of lung cancer — and SIADH is one of its classic endocrine syndromes.

Small cell carcinoma profile:
• Central, perihilar mass in a heavy smoker; highly anaplastic small blue cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding
• Neuroendocrine origin — chromogranin and synaptophysin positive
• Paraneoplastic: SIADH (hyponatremia), Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH), Lambert-Eaton syndrome (anti-P/Q calcium channel antibodies)
• Chemotherapy responsive initially but micrometastatic at diagnosis — surgery is rarely an option

Contrast: squamous cell carcinoma gives PTHrP hypercalcemia and is also central; adenocarcinoma is peripheral and the most common histology overall

Mnemonic: Small cell = Small sodium (SIADH) and Small blue cells
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 10; Robbins 9/e p716

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 11: Kidney and Urinary Bladder
questions.stem: Electron microscopy in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis shows:

options.text: Effacement of podocyte foot processes alone

questions.explanation:
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the lumpy-bumpy immune complex disease of childhood nephritic syndrome — and the humps are its EM signature.

PSGN diagnostic picture:
• Light microscopy — enlarged hypercellular glomeruli stuffed with neutrophils
• Immunofluorescence — granular (lumpy-bumpy) deposits of IgG and C3
• Electron microscopy — discrete subepithelial hump-shaped deposits on the outer GBM
• Clinical — tea or cola colored urine, RBC casts, periorbital edema, hypertension, low C3 that normalizes in 6–8 weeks
• Preceded 1–4 weeks earlier by group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo

Why not the others:
• Subendothelial deposits — lupus nephritis (wire loops)
• Foot process effacement alone — minimal change disease
• Linear IgG — Goodpasture syndrome

Mnemonic: PSGN Puts Party Humps on the Podocyte roof (subEPIthelial = Epic roof)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 11; Robbins 9/e p911

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 11: Kidney and Urinary Bladder
questions.stem: The most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children is:
questions.explanation:
Minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis) is the dominant nephrotic syndrome of childhood — up to 80% of pediatric cases.

Minimal change disease essentials:
• Light microscopy — glomeruli look normal (hence minimal change); lipoid droplets in tubules gave the old name
• Electron microscopy — the only abnormality: diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes
• Immunofluorescence — negative (no deposits)
• Cause — often post-viral or atopic (T cell cytokine, permeability factor) and linked to Hodgkin lymphoma and NSAIDs
• Response — exquisitely steroid responsive; most children recover completely

Contrast by age:
• Children — minimal change disease
• Adults — membranous nephropathy (most common in Caucasians), FSGS (most common in African Americans)

Mnemonic: MCD = Mostly Children's Disease (and Minimal under the microscope)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 11; Robbins 9/e p903

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 11: Kidney and Urinary Bladder
questions.stem: A 55-year-old smoker with hematuria, flank pain and a palpable renal mass has a tumor arising from the renal tubular epithelium with clear cytoplasm. The gene implicated is:
questions.explanation:
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma — the most common renal malignancy of adults — is driven by inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p.

VHL gene biology:
• Normal VHL degrades HIF-1 alpha; when VHL is lost, HIF-1 alpha accumulates and switches on angiogenesis (VEGF) and erythropoietin
• Explains the paraneoplastic trio of polycythemia (EPO), hypertension (renin) and hypervascularity
• Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome — bilateral clear cell RCC plus hemangioblastomas and pheochromocytoma

Classic clinical triad (rare but exam-famous):
• Hematuria, palpable mass, dull flank pain
• Left-sided tumors can compress the left renal vein causing a left varicocele

Why not the others:
• APC — colon polyposis; RET — MEN2 and medullary thyroid cancer; BRCA2 — breast and prostate

Mnemonic: Clear cell RCC = Van Hippel-Lindau on chromosome 3 (VHL — the Kidney's gatekeeper)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 11; Robbins 9/e p953

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 12: Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: The most common cause of duodenal peptic ulcer disease worldwide is:
questions.explanation:
Helicobacter pylori is the undisputed heavyweight of peptic ulcer disease — it colonizes roughly 70–90% of duodenal ulcer patients.

How H. pylori earns its ulcer:
• Flagella, urease and adhesins let it burrow into gastric-type epithelium
• Urease splits urea into ammonia — buffers acid and powers the breath test
• Vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA) and cytotoxin-associated antigen (CagA) damage epithelium
• Chronic gastritis → peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal type) and MALT lymphoma

Contrast:
• NSAIDs are the second major cause — and the dominant one in H. pylori-negative ulcers
• Zollinger-Ellison — gastrinoma with multiple, distal and refractory ulcers

Mnemonic: H. pylori Holds the H for Ulcer Helicity — urease test, breath test, biopsy
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 12; Robbins 9/e p771

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 12: Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: Barrett esophagus is best described as:

options.text: Squamous metaplasia of the distal esophagus
Intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus

questions.answerText: Intestinal metaplasia of the distal esophagus
questions.explanation:
Chronic gastroesophageal reflux forces the squamous lining of the lower esophagus to transform into acid-resistant intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells — Barrett esophagus.

Why it matters:
• It is a premalignant lesion — risk of esophageal ADENOCARCINOMA is 30 to 60 times the normal population
• Requires endoscopic surveillance with four-quadrant biopsies
• Dysplasia progression: low-grade → high-grade → invasive adenocarcinoma

Look for:
• Tongues of salmon-pink mucosa extending above the gastroesophageal junction
• Goblet cells on biopsy — the histological requirement

Epidemiology: middle-aged to elderly white men with long-standing GERD, central obesity, and smoking

Mnemonic: Barrett Builds (metaplastic) Bowls — Goblet cells Guard the Gerd-damaged gut
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 12; Robbins 9/e p757

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 12: Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: All of the following favor Crohn disease over ulcerative colitis EXCEPT:

options.text: Continuous involvement starting from the rectum

questions.answerText: Continuous involvement starting from the rectum
questions.explanation:
Continuous inflammation that always begins in the rectum and extends proximally is the signature of ulcerative colitis — every other listed feature belongs to Crohn disease.

Crohn disease fingerprint:
• Skip lesions with normal mucosa between diseased segments
• Transmural inflammation — the whole wall is angry (fistulae, strictures, creeping fat)
• Non-caseating granulomas in up to 35% of cases
• Anywhere from mouth to anus, but the terminal ileum is the favorite site
• Cobblestone mucosa, string sign of Kantor on barium, aphthous to linear ulcers

Ulcerative colitis fingerprint:
• Continuous, starts at the rectum, limited to the mucosa and submucosa
• Pseudopolyps, lead-pipe colon, high risk of cholangiocarcinoma-sclerosing cholangitis association and colorectal cancer

Mnemonic: CROhn = CRew of features — skips, whole-wall, granulomas; UC = Uninterrupted, Confined to mucosa
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 12; Robbins 9/e p800

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 12: Gastrointestinal Tract
questions.stem: The most specific serological marker for celiac disease is:
questions.explanation:
Anti-tTG IgA is the first-line screen for celiac disease — highly sensitive and specific, easy to automate, and its titer falls with a gluten-free diet (a built-in monitor of compliance).

Celiac disease package:
• Gliadin peptides deamidated by tissue transglutaminase become antigenic in HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 individuals
• Biopsy (the gold standard): villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in the proximal small bowel
• Anti-endomysial antibody targets the same tTG antigen but uses monkey esophagus substrate — better as a confirmatory test
• Associations — dermatitis herpetiformis, type 1 diabetes, IgA deficiency (false-negative tTG IgA)

Mnemonic: Celiac = tTG Tells (screen); gluten GONE makes titers Go down
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 12; Robbins 9/e p783

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 13: Liver
questions.stem: The most common cause of portal hypertension worldwide is:
questions.explanation:
Cirrhosis — whatever its cause — is the leading cause of portal hypertension across the globe, because fibrotic bands strangle the intrahepatic vasculature and regenerative nodules compress the sinusoids.

Classification of portal hypertension:
• Intrahepatic (presinusoidal) — schistosomiasis, primary biliary cholangitis, sarcoidosis
• Intrahepatic (post-sinusoidal) — cirrhosis, the commonest cause in practice
• Post-hepatic — Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis
• Prehepatic — portal vein thrombosis

Consequences of portal hypertension:
• Esophageal varices (bleeding is the deadliest), caput medusae, hemorrhoids
• Ascites, splenomegaly with hypersplenism

Mnemonic: Cirrhosis CompresSes the sinusoids — the Commonest Cause
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 13; Robbins 9/e p829

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 13: Liver
questions.stem: A young patient with cirrhosis has a golden-brown ring at the corneal limbus, tremors and low serum ceruloplasmin. The defective gene is:
questions.explanation:
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive copper-storage disorder caused by ATP7B mutations — the copper transporter that normally escorts excess copper into bile and onto ceruloplasmin.

Wilson disease presentation:
• Kayser-Fleischer ring — copper in Descemet membrane at the corneal limbus
• Neurology — tremors, dysarthria, dystonia, psychiatric change (a treatable movement disorder!)
• Liver — cirrhosis in a young person, sometimes fulminant hepatitis with Coombs negative hemolysis
• Labs — LOW ceruloplasmin, high urinary copper, high hepatic copper

Treatment: copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine plus dietary copper restriction and zinc

Why not the others:
• HFE — hemochromatosis (iron); SERPINA1 — alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; CFTR — cystic fibrosis

Mnemonic: ATP7B — 7 letters B for both Bile and Brain; chromosome 13 like a Baker's dozen of copper coins
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 13; Robbins 9/e p852

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 13: Liver
questions.stem: A woman on oral contraceptives presents with sudden right upper quadrant pain, ascites and massive hepatomegaly. Doppler shows hepatic vein thrombosis. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Budd-Chiari syndrome is the clinical syndrome of hepatic venous outflow obstruction — thrombosis of the hepatic veins or the inferior vena cava.

Classic triad:
• Abdominal pain — sudden right upper quadrant ache
• Ascites — often tense and protein-rich
• Massive tender hepatomegaly

Risk factors:
• Hypercoagulable states — oral contraceptives, pregnancy, polycythemia vera, factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
• The centrolobular congestion and sinusoidal dilatation produce the characteristic nutmeg liver

Why not the others:
• Zieve — hemolysis and hypertriglyceridemia with alcoholic hepatitis
• Reye — aspirin-associated microvesicular steatosis in children
• Hepatorenal — functional renal failure of advanced cirrhosis, no vein thrombosis

Mnemonic: Budd-Chiari Blocks the Blood highway — Pain, Ascites, Big liver (the PAB triad)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 13; Robbins 9/e p854

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 13: Liver
questions.stem: Microvesicular fatty change with mitochondrial injury in a child treated with aspirin for a viral illness is characteristic of:
questions.explanation:
Reye syndrome is the devastating aspirin-triggered mitochondrial hepatopathy of children recovering from influenza or varicella.

Key features:
• Microvesicular steatosis — tiny fat droplets pack the hepatocyte cytoplasm around a central nucleus
• Mitochondrial injury blocks beta-oxidation and the urea cycle
• Hepatic encephalopathy with a razor-sharp rise in ammonia, hypoglycemia and elevated short-chain fatty acids
• Elevated AST/ALT with typically near-normal bilirubin — the liver fails metabolically, not excretorily

Prevention: avoiding aspirin in febrile children has virtually eliminated the disease

Why not the others:
• Acute fatty liver of pregnancy — same microvesicular pattern but in the third trimester (defect in mitochondrial beta-oxidation enzymes)
• Wilson — copper storage; alcoholic hepatitis — macrovesicular steatosis with neutrophils and Mallory bodies

Mnemonic: Reye = aspiRin + vIRus in the Young — microvesicular Mitochondrial Mayhem
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 13; Robbins 9/e p853

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 14: Genital System and Breast
questions.stem: Koilocytosis of the cervical epithelium is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Koilocytes — squamous cells with perinuclear halos and wrinkled raisin-like nuclei — are the cytopathic calling card of human papillomavirus on Pap smear and biopsy.

HPV essentials:
• High-risk types 16 and 18 drive most cervical squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma
• E6 protein degrades p53; E7 protein inactivates RB1 — the viral oncogenic engine
• Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminatum (genital warts)
• Dysplasia ladder: CIN 1 (koilocytosis) → CIN 2 → CIN 3 (carcinoma in situ)

Why not the others:
• HSV — multinucleation, nuclear molding, Cowdry A inclusions
• CMV — owl-eye intranuclear inclusions
• Trichomonas — pear-shaped flagellates with inflammation, no koilocytosis

Mnemonic: Koilo = hollow — the HPV halo; E6 kills p53, E7 frees RB
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 14; Robbins 9/e p1009

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 14: Genital System and Breast
questions.stem: The most common benign tumor of the breast in a 20-year-old woman is:
questions.explanation:
Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor of young women — a firm, rubbery, freely mobile lump that bounces under the fingers (the breast mouse).

Fibroadenoma profile:
• Age — usually 15 to 30 years
• Hormone sensitive — may enlarge during pregnancy and regress after menopause
• Histology — a benign proliferation of stromal cells compressing glandular spaces into slits (pericanalicular or intracanalicular patterns)
• Behavior — does NOT transform into cancer (unlike a phyllodes tumor, its giant cousin)

Contrast:
• Phyllodes tumor — older women, leaf-like stromal overgrowth, can be malignant and recurs locally
• Intraductal papilloma — bloody nipple discharge in peri-menopausal women

Mnemonic: Fibroadenoma is the Friendly Freely mobile Friend of the twenties
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 14; Robbins 9/e p1046

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 14: Genital System and Breast
questions.stem: The most important risk factor for endometrial carcinoma is:
questions.explanation:
Endometrial carcinoma grows in an estrogen bath without the protective brake of progesterone — unopposed estrogen is the single most important driver.

Sources of unopposed estrogen:
• Obesity — adipose aromatase converts androgens to estrogen
• Anovulatory cycles and polycystic ovarian disease
• Estrogen-secreting granulosa-theca cell tumors
• Delayed menopause, tamoxifen therapy
• Estrogen replacement therapy without progestins

Protective factors (the mirror image):
• Combined oral contraceptives, multiparity, progestin use — all reduce risk

Subtypes:
• Type 1 — endometrioid, estrogen-driven, low grade, good prognosis
• Type 2 — serous, p53 mutated, elderly, aggressive

Mnemonic: Unopposed Estrogen = Uninterrupted Entry ticket for the carcinoma
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 14; Robbins 9/e p1016

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 14: Genital System and Breast
questions.stem: Prostatic adenocarcinoma most commonly arises from which zone of the prostate?
questions.explanation:
The peripheral zone is where most prostatic adenocarcinomas arise — which is why digital rectal examination can feel them and why they are silent early.

Zone-wise pathology of the prostate:
• Peripheral zone — 70–80% of carcinomas; palpable on DRE, accessed by biopsy
• Transition zone — benign prostatic hyperplasia and about 20% of cancers (the TURP specimens)
• Central zone — rarely cancerous (resistant zone)

Tumor biology:
• Acinar adenocarcinoma with Gleason grading of architectural pattern
• Osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases — elevated alkaline phosphatase
• PSA screening and histological diagnosis by needle biopsy

Mnemonic: Cancer lives on the Periphery — BPH Bulges in the middle (Transition)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 14; Robbins 9/e p983

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 15: Central Nervous System
questions.stem: Neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer disease are composed of:
questions.explanation:
Neurofibrillary tangles are intracellular ropes of hyperphosphorylated tau — a microtubule-associated protein that has slipped its moorings.

Alzheimer pathology scorecard:
• Neurofibrillary tangles — intracellular, paired helical filaments of hyperphosphorylated tau; their density in the hippocampus correlates best with dementia severity
• Neuritic plaques — extracellular beta-amyloid cores (A-beta 42) surrounded by dystrophic neurites
• Amyloid angiopathy, granulovacuolar degeneration, loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert

Why not the others:
• Beta-amyloid — the plaque core, not the tangle
• Alpha-synuclein — Lewy bodies of Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies

Mnemonic: Tangles = Tau inside (T and T); Plaques = Amyloid outside (A and A)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 15; Robbins 9/e p1306

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 15: Central Nervous System
questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity and a pill-rolling tremor died of pneumonia. Brain biopsy of the substantia nigra would show:

options.text: Lewy bodies with loss of pigmented neurons

questions.answerText: Lewy bodies with loss of pigmented neurons
questions.explanation:
Parkinson disease depigments the substantia nigra — dopaminergic neurons die and leave behind Lewy bodies, the intracytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein.

Parkinson pathology:
• Gross — pallor of the substantia nigra and locus ceruleus
• Micro — loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons with gliosis and Lewy bodies (eosinophilic, alpha-synuclein positive, ubiquitin positive)
• Clinical triad — resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia (TRAP: Tremor at rest, Rigidity, Akinesia, Postural instability)
• Treatment logic — levodopa replaces the dying dopamine supply

Why not the others:
• Pseudopalisading necrosis — glioblastoma multiforme
• Neurofibrillary tangles — Alzheimer disease
• Negri bodies — rabies

Mnemonic: Parkinson's Pigment Perishes, leaving alpha-synuclein Pebbles (Lewy bodies)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 15; Robbins 9/e p1324

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 15: Central Nervous System
questions.stem: The histological hallmark of glioblastoma multiforme is:
questions.explanation:
Glioblastoma multiforme is the most malignant astrocytoma (WHO grade 4), and pseudopalisading necrosis plus microvascular proliferation are its two pathognomonic features.

GBM essentials:
• Tumor cells line up in palisades around geographic necrotic zones — pseudopalisading necrosis
• Exuberant endothelial and smooth muscle proliferation of vessels — microvascular (glomeruloid) proliferation
• Crosses the midline through the corpus callosum — the butterfly glioma
• Molecular hallmarks — EGFR amplification, MGMT methylation status guides temozolomide response
• Prognosis — grim: median survival of about a year even with surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide

Why not the others:
• Perivascular rosettes — ependymoma and medulloblastoma
• Psammoma bodies — meningioma, papillary thyroid carcinoma

Mnemonic: GBM = Girdles the midline, Butterfly wings, Multiforme mayhem — necrosis with a picket fence
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 15; Robbins 9/e p1338

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 16: Endocrine System
questions.stem: A thyroid carcinoma with Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies, occurring in a young woman with excellent prognosis, is:
questions.explanation:
Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy — and the friendliest, with a 20-year survival above 90%.

Papillary carcinoma fingerprint:
• Orphan Annie eye nuclei — optically clear, ground-glass nuclei with nuclear grooves and intranuclear pseudoinclusions (the diagnosis is cytological, not architectural)
• Psammoma bodies — concentric lamellated calcifications
• Papillary architecture with fibrovascular cores; lymphatic spread to cervical nodes common yet paradoxically prognosis stays excellent
• Risk factor — childhood neck irradiation
• Treatment — surgical resection; responds to TSH suppression and radioiodine

Why not the others:
• Follicular — hematogenous spread, angioinvasion, no psammoma bodies
• Medullary — C cells, amyloid stroma, calcitonin, MEN2 with RET
• Anaplastic — elderly, lethal within months

Mnemonic: Papillary = Pretty Prognosis with Pseudoinclusions and Psammoma (all P's)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 16; Robbins 9/e p1100

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 16: Endocrine System
questions.stem: A patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and mucosal neuromas has which germline mutation?
questions.explanation:
The triad of medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and mucosal neuromas is MEN2B — one of the RET proto-oncogene syndromes on chromosome 10.

MEN syndromes map:
• MEN1 (Wermer) — pituitary, parathyroid, pancreas (the 3 Ps) — MEN1 gene
• MEN2A (Sipple) — medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia — RET
• MEN2B — MEN2A pattern without parathyroid disease, plus mucosal neuromas and Marfanoid habitus — RET (more aggressive)

Why RET matters:
• Activating germline mutations — prophylactic thyroidectomy is planned in childhood once the mutation is found
• Genotype-phenotype correlation is so tight that a single codon predicts the clinical course

Mnemonic: RET = Really Every Tumor (medullary thyroid + pheo + neuromas); MEN1 = the 3 Ps
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 16; Robbins 9/e p1136

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 16: Endocrine System
questions.stem: The rule of 10s applies to all of the following about pheochromocytoma EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
The rule of 10s packages the memorable minority features of pheochromocytoma — but the catecholamine secretory pattern is not one of them.

The rule of 10s:
• 10% are extra-adrenal (organ of Zuckerkandl, paragangliomas)
• 10% are bilateral (much higher in familial syndromes — MEN2, VHL, NF1)
• 10% are malignant (metastases, not histology, define malignancy)
• 10% are familial, 10% occur in children, 10% are calcified, 10% recur

Secretory pattern (why the exception is right):
• Nearly ALL secrete norepinephrine with or without epinephrine — epinephrine alone is distinctly uncommon
• Paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations with hypertension is the classic triad
• Diagnosis — 24-hour urinary metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive)

Mnemonic: 10-10-10 extra-adrenal, bilateral, malignant — but adrenaline alone? Never the norm
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 16; Robbins 9/e p1131

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 17: Musculoskeletal System
questions.stem: The mosaic or jigsaw-puzzle pattern of lamellar bone with frantic osteoclastic activity is characteristic of:
questions.explanation:
Paget disease is a localized disorder of chaotic bone remodeling — osteoclasts dig too deep, osteoblasts patch too fast, and the result is architecturally disorganized mosaic bone.

Phases of Paget disease:
• Lytic (osteolytic) — giant multinucleated osteoclasts with up to 100 nuclei resorb bone
• Mixed — frantic osteoblastic repair begins while lysis continues
• Sclerotic (burnt out) — thick, disorganized trabeculae with the classic mosaic (jigsaw) cement lines

Clinical anchors:
• Elevated serum ALP with NORMAL calcium and phosphate
• Triad of presentations — skull involvement (osteoclastoma-like lesions, hearing loss), long bone bowing, pelvic pain
• Sarcomatous transformation in about 1% — osteosarcoma risk

Mnemonic: Paget = Patches of Panic — osteoclasts overreact, osteoblasts overpatch, mosaic remains
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 17; Robbins 9/e p1187

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 17: Musculoskeletal System
questions.stem: Joint aspirate from a patient with acute monoarthritis shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals under polarized light. The diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Monosodium urate monohydrate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly NEGATIVELY birefringent — yellow when parallel to the slow axis of the red compensator — and they define gout.

Crystal atlas of arthritis:
• Gout — needle-shaped, negatively birefringent, MSU; first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is the classic first strike
• Pseudogout — rhomboid-shaped, POSITIVELY birefringent calcium pyrophosphate; knee of an elderly patient

Pathophysiology of gout:
• Hyperuricemia from overproduction (HGPRT deficiency in Lesch-Nyhan, PRPP synthetase) or underexcretion (renal, thiazides)
• Tophi, urate nephropathy and uric acid stones round out the picture
• Acute treatment — NSAIDs, colchicine; chronic — allopurinol or febuxostat (never started during an acute flare)

Mnemonic: Gout = Needles that Negative-birefract; Pseudogout = Positively birefringent Pebbles (rhomboid)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 17; Robbins 9/e p1222

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 18: Miscellaneous
questions.stem: Tissue amyloid stained with Congo red shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. This property is due to:

options.text: Random coil structure of the deposits

questions.explanation:
All amyloid fibrils — whatever their precursor protein — share a beta-pleated sheet architecture, which is what gives Congo red its magical apple-green birefringence.

Amyloid essentials:
• Structure — non-branching 7.5 to 10 nm fibrils in beta-pleated sheets, insoluble and proteolysis resistant
• Stains — Congo red (apple-green under polarized light), metachromatic with crystal violet, positive with thioflavin T
• Types — AL (light chains, plasma cell dyscrasias), AA (secondary to chronic inflammation), ATTR (transthyretin, senile cardiac and familial forms), beta-2 microglobulin (dialysis related)

Clinical anchors:
• Kidney — the most commonly involved organ, nephrotic range proteinuria
• Heart — restrictive cardiomyopathy with echo showing speckled appearance
• Tongue macroglossia — think AL amyloidosis

Mnemonic: Amyloid Always Adopts the A-fold (antiparallel beta-pleated sheets) — hence the Apple-green Answer
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 18; Robbins 9/e p250

questions.src: Review of Pathology and Genetics, 8/e (Garg & Gupta) · Chapter 18: Miscellaneous
questions.stem: The antibody most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus is:
questions.explanation:
Anti-dsDNA antibodies are the most SPECIFIC marker for SLE and track with disease activity and lupus nephritis — while ANA is merely the most SENSITIVE screen.

SLE antibody hierarchy:
• ANA — most sensitive (>95%), great for screening but nonspecific
• Anti-dsDNA — most specific, correlates with nephritis and flares
• Anti-Sm — essentially 100% specific but only 10–30% sensitive; a diagnostic trophy, not a monitor
• Anti-Ro/SSA — neonatal lupus with congenital heart block, Sjogren overlap
• Anti-phospholipid antibodies — anticoagulant paradox (positive aPTT with thrombosis)

Contrast: rheumatoid factor belongs to rheumatoid arthritis and can be falsely positive in many other states

Mnemonic: dsDNA = Disease activity and DNA damage tracking; Sm = the Smoking gun (specific but rare)
Reference: Garg & Gupta, Review of Pathology and Genetics 8/e, Ch 18; Robbins 9/e p216
